history.q: According to tradition, in which year was Rome founded?
history.fact: Legend says Romulus founded Rome on 21 April 753 BCE, and the city still celebrates that date as its birthday, the Natale di Roma.

history.q: Which general led the 1860 'Expedition of the Thousand' that helped unify Italy?
history.fact: Garibaldi's volunteers, nicknamed the 'Redshirts', sailed from near Genoa in 1860 and went on to conquer Sicily and Naples.

history.q: In which year did the eruption of Mount Vesuvius bury Pompeii?
history.fact: Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters; his uncle, Pliny the Elder, died while leading a rescue mission across the bay.

history.q: Which banking family dominated Renaissance Florence and patronised artists like Michelangelo?
history.fact: The Medici produced popes Leo X and Clement VII and two queens of France, Catherine and Marie de' Medici.

history.q: Who became Rome's first emperor in 27 BCE?
history.fact: The month of August is named after Augustus; Julius Caesar, his great-uncle, was dictator but never emperor.

history.q: Who became the first King of a unified Italy in 1861?
history.fact: Rome's enormous white Vittoriano monument, jokingly nicknamed 'the wedding cake' or 'the typewriter', was built in his honour.

history.q: Which Germanic leader deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman emperor, in 476 CE?
history.fact: The deposed teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus was not killed but pensioned off to live in a villa near Naples.

history.q: In which year did Mussolini's Fascists stage the 'March on Rome'?
history.fact: King Victor Emmanuel III invited Mussolini to form a government; Mussolini himself arrived in Rome by overnight train from Milan.

history.q: Which city was the capital of the Kingdom of Italy from 1865 to 1871, before Rome?
history.fact: Italy's capital moved from Turin to Florence in 1865, then to Rome in 1871 after the city was taken from the Papal States.

history.q: In which year did mutinous troops of Emperor Charles V carry out the infamous Sack of Rome?
history.fact: During the sack, Pope Clement VII fled along a fortified passage to Castel Sant'Angelo while the Swiss Guard fought a heroic rearguard.

history.q: Which Roman leader was assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BCE?
history.fact: Caesar was stabbed 23 times at a Senate meeting held in the Curia of Pompey, because the usual Senate House was being rebuilt.

history.q: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with war elephants to invade Italy in 218 BCE?
history.fact: Hannibal crushed a much larger Roman army at Cannae in 216 BCE, yet he never captured Rome itself.

history.q: Which emperor ruled Rome when much of the city burned in the Great Fire of 64 CE?
history.fact: The tale that Nero 'fiddled while Rome burned' is legend: the fiddle did not exist yet, and Tacitus says he was at Antium when the fire began.

history.q: Which Venetian merchant described his travels to the court of Kublai Khan in China?
history.fact: Marco Polo dictated his travels to a writer of romances, Rustichello da Pisa, while both were prisoners of war in Genoa.

history.q: In which Italian port city was Christopher Columbus born?
history.fact: Columbus sailed for Spain: his 1492 voyage was sponsored by Ferdinand and Isabella, and he died in 1506 still believing he had reached Asia.

history.q: Which emperor, together with his co-emperor Licinius, issued the Edict of Milan in 313 CE granting tolerance to Christians?
history.fact: Constantine later refounded the old Greek city of Byzantium as Constantinople, dedicating it as his new capital in 330 CE.

history.q: Which Roman emperor ordered a defensive wall built across northern Britain from 122 CE?
history.fact: Hadrian's Wall ran about 117 km from coast to coast; his successor Antoninus Pius later built a second wall further north.

history.q: Which Italian maritime republic was led by an elected Doge for over a thousand years?
history.fact: The last Doge, Ludovico Manin, abdicated in 1797 when Napoleon's army brought the Venetian Republic to an end.

history.q: Which Dominican friar organised the 'Bonfire of the Vanities' in Florence in 1497?
history.fact: Savonarola was himself executed and burned in Florence's Piazza della Signoria in 1498; a plaque in the square marks the spot.

history.q: In which year did Italy enter the Second World War on Germany's side?
history.fact: Italy declared war on 10 June 1940; after Mussolini's fall it signed an armistice with the Allies, announced on 8 September 1943.

history.q: At which 1176 battle did the Lombard League defeat Emperor Frederick Barbarossa?
history.fact: The victory is remembered in Italy's national anthem, which declares that from the Alps to Sicily 'everywhere is Legnano'.

history.q: What name is given to the 1282 uprising in Sicily against the rule of Charles of Anjou?
history.fact: The revolt reputedly began outside a Palermo church at the hour of vespers on Easter Monday, and later inspired an opera by Verdi.

history.q: Which secret 1915 treaty brought Italy into the First World War on the Allied side?
history.fact: Italy had been in the Triple Alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary, but stayed neutral in 1914 before switching sides in May 1915.

history.q: Which Roman general defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE?
history.fact: Scipio took the name 'Africanus' from his victory; his adoptive grandson, Scipio Aemilianus, destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE.

history.q: The 'Five Days of Milan' in March 1848 was an uprising against which power?
history.fact: Field Marshal Radetzky withdrew from Milan but retook it that August; Johann Strauss I's Radetzky March was written in his honour.

technology.q: Guglielmo Marconi is best known for pioneering which technology?
technology.fact: Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics, and in 1901 sent a radio signal across the Atlantic from Cornwall to Newfoundland.

technology.q: Alessandro Volta's 'voltaic pile' of 1800 was the first what?
technology.fact: The unit of electric potential, the volt, is named in Volta's honour; Napoleon later made him a count.

technology.q: In 1610, which scientist discovered four large moons of Jupiter with his telescope?
technology.fact: Galileo named the moons the 'Medicean Stars' to flatter his patrons; today Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto are called the Galilean moons.

technology.q: Which Renaissance genius filled notebooks with designs for flying machines, written in mirror script?
technology.fact: One of Leonardo's notebooks, the Codex Leicester, was bought by Bill Gates in 1994 for about 30 million dollars.

technology.q: Which Italian physicist led the team that achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in 1942?
technology.fact: Chicago Pile-1 was built under the stands of a university sports field; the element fermium is named after Fermi.

technology.q: Which Paduan instrument maker invented the piano around 1700 in Florence?
technology.fact: Cristofori's instrument could play soft and loud, hence 'pianoforte'; his 1720 piano at New York's Met is the oldest surviving one.

technology.q: Evangelista Torricelli invented which instrument in 1643?
technology.fact: Torricelli had been Galileo's assistant; a unit of pressure, the torr, is named after him.

technology.q: In which city was the carmaker FIAT founded in 1899?
technology.fact: FIAT stands for Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino; its old Lingotto factory famously had a test track on its roof.

technology.q: Which Italian chemist shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on polymers such as polypropylene?
technology.fact: Natta's team in Milan made isotactic polypropylene in 1954, a tough plastic now found in everything from car bumpers to food tubs.

technology.q: Rita Levi-Montalcini won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Medicine for discovering what?
technology.fact: Barred from university by Fascist racial laws, she ran experiments on chick embryos in a lab in her bedroom; she lived to 103.

technology.q: Which Italian carmaker uses a black prancing horse as its emblem?
technology.fact: The prancing horse was the emblem of First World War fighter ace Francesco Baracca; his mother suggested Enzo Ferrari use it for luck.

technology.q: Which medieval mathematician from Pisa gives his name to the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13...?
technology.fact: In his 1202 book Liber Abaci, Fibonacci used the sequence to model breeding rabbits, and helped spread Hindu-Arabic numerals across Europe.

technology.q: What material did the Romans use to build the Pantheon's great dome, the largest unreinforced dome of its kind?
technology.fact: Roman concrete used volcanic ash called pozzolana; harbour structures built with it have survived 2,000 years of pounding seawater.

technology.q: Which Italian scooter, launched by Piaggio in 1946, takes its name from the Italian word for 'wasp'?
technology.fact: Enrico Piaggio reportedly named it after its buzzing engine; Audrey Hepburn and Gregory Peck rode one in the film 'Roman Holiday' (1953).

technology.q: Which Italian company created Nutella, the hazelnut and cocoa spread?
technology.fact: Nutella grew out of Pietro Ferrero's 1946 'Giandujot', which stretched scarce cocoa with Piedmont hazelnuts; the Nutella name arrived in 1964.

technology.q: Which Bologna scientist's experiments with twitching frogs' legs led him to propose 'animal electricity'?
technology.fact: The word 'galvanise' comes from his name; his rival Volta argued the electricity came from the metals, not the frog.

technology.q: Which Turin scientist proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules?
technology.fact: Avogadro's idea was largely ignored until Stanislao Cannizzaro championed it at the 1860 Karlsruhe Congress, four years after Avogadro's death.

technology.q: Which Italian company launched the Programma 101, one of the first desktop programmable computers, in 1965?
technology.fact: NASA used Programma 101 machines for calculations while planning the 1969 Apollo 11 Moon landing.

technology.q: The Milan company Pirelli, founded in 1872, is best known for making what?
technology.fact: Pirelli has been the sole tyre supplier to Formula One since 2011, and also publishes a famous annual photography calendar.

technology.q: The Fallopian tubes are named after which 16th-century Italian anatomist?
technology.fact: Falloppio held the chair of anatomy at the University of Padua, where the great Andreas Vesalius had lectured before him.

technology.q: Which Italian scientist first observed capillaries, through a microscope, in 1661?
technology.fact: Seeing capillaries in a frog's lung supplied the missing link between arteries and veins in William Harvey's theory of blood circulation.

technology.q: Which Milanese polymath published methods for solving cubic and quartic equations in his 1545 book 'Ars Magna'?
technology.fact: Cardano had promised Niccolò Tartaglia to keep his cubic method secret, sparking a bitter feud when it appeared in print.

technology.q: Who invented the stovetop moka pot in 1933?
technology.fact: The Bialetti logo's moustachioed little man is a caricature of Alfonso's son Renato, whose ashes were buried in a giant moka pot in 2016.

technology.q: Which Italian-born physicist shared the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering the antiproton?
technology.fact: Segrè also co-discovered technetium in 1937, the first chemical element to be produced artificially.

technology.q: Which Italian-born engineer designed the chip of the Intel 4004 (1971), the first commercially available microprocessor?
technology.fact: Faggin etched his initials 'F.F.' onto the 4004's silicon; he later co-founded Zilog, maker of the hugely popular Z80 chip.

art.q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
art.fact: Michelangelo painted the ceiling between 1508 and 1512, though he always considered himself first and foremost a sculptor.

art.q: Who painted 'The Last Supper' on a refectory wall in Milan?
art.fact: Leonardo experimented with paint on dry plaster, so it began flaking in his lifetime; sandbags helped it survive a 1943 bombing raid.

art.q: Who wrote the 'Divine Comedy'?
art.fact: Dante simply called it 'Commedia'; the word 'Divina' was added later, popularised by Boccaccio's praise of the poem.

art.q: Which composer wrote the operas 'Aida' and 'La Traviata'?
art.fact: Aida had its world premiere in Cairo in 1871, at the Khedivial Opera House.

art.q: Who painted 'The Birth of Venus'?
art.fact: The Birth of Venus hangs in Florence's Uffizi Gallery, close to Botticelli's other great mythological painting, Primavera.

art.q: The aria 'Nessun dorma' comes from which Puccini opera?
art.fact: Puccini died before finishing Turandot; at the 1926 premiere, conductor Toscanini stopped the performance where Puccini's music ended.

art.q: Which Venetian composer wrote 'The Four Seasons'?
art.fact: Vivaldi, an ordained priest nicknamed 'the Red Priest' for his red hair, taught music at a Venetian orphanage for girls.

art.q: Which director made the 1960 film 'La Dolce Vita'?
art.fact: The film's celebrity photographer, Paparazzo, gave the world the word 'paparazzi'.

art.q: Which architect designed the great dome of Florence Cathedral?
art.fact: Built between 1420 and 1436 without a wooden support frame, it remains the largest brick dome ever constructed.

art.q: Which Baroque painter, famed for dramatic light and shadow, painted 'The Calling of Saint Matthew' in Rome?
art.fact: Caravaggio's life was as dramatic as his art: he fled Rome in 1606 after killing a man in a brawl.

art.q: In which city can visitors see Michelangelo's original marble statue of David?
art.fact: Carved from a block of marble other sculptors had abandoned, David stood outdoors in Piazza della Signoria until 1873; a replica stands there now.

art.q: Which composer wrote the operas 'La Bohème' and 'Madama Butterfly'?
art.fact: Puccini came from a long line of church musicians in Lucca; a festival of his operas is held each summer at Torre del Lago, where he lived.

art.q: Which Renaissance artist painted 'The School of Athens' in the Vatican?
art.fact: Raphael is widely thought to have used Leonardo da Vinci as his model for Plato, and he painted his own face among the crowd.

art.q: Which tenor from Modena sang as one of the 'Three Tenors' with Plácido Domingo and José Carreras?
art.fact: At New York's Met in 1972, Pavarotti hit nine high Cs in a single aria, earning the nickname 'King of the High Cs'.

art.q: Which Milan opera house, opened in 1778, is one of the most famous in the world?
art.fact: La Scala takes its name from the church of Santa Maria alla Scala, which was demolished to make way for the theatre.

art.q: Who wrote 'The Adventures of Pinocchio'?
art.fact: Collodi was a pen name taken from his mother's Tuscan village; the author's real name was Carlo Lorenzini.

art.q: Which Venetian master painted the 'Venus of Urbino'?
art.fact: Titian worked for over 60 years and was still painting when he died in Venice during the plague of 1576.

art.q: Which Baroque sculptor created 'The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa' and Rome's Fountain of the Four Rivers?
art.fact: Bernini also designed the sweeping colonnades that embrace St Peter's Square like a pair of open arms.

art.q: Who directed and starred in the 1997 film 'Life Is Beautiful'?
art.fact: Benigni won the Best Actor Oscar for the role, famously clambering over the seats of the audience on his way to the stage.

art.q: Which composer wrote the opera 'The Barber of Seville' (1816)?
art.fact: Rossini retired from opera aged 37 after 'William Tell' and devoted himself to food; the dish tournedos Rossini is named after him.

art.q: Which painter decorated Padua's Scrovegni Chapel with a celebrated fresco cycle in the early 1300s?
art.fact: Giotto also designed Florence Cathedral's bell tower, still known today as Giotto's Campanile.

art.q: Who wrote the novel 'The Leopard' (Il Gattopardo), published in 1958?
art.fact: Published after its author's death, it became a bestseller and was filmed by Luchino Visconti in 1963 with Burt Lancaster.

art.q: Which director made the Neorealist classic 'Bicycle Thieves' (1948)?
art.fact: De Sica cast non-professional actors; his lead, Lamberto Maggiorani, was a factory worker.

art.q: Which Neoclassical sculptor created 'Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss', now in the Louvre?
art.fact: Canova also sculpted Napoleon's sister Pauline Bonaparte reclining as Venus, now in Rome's Galleria Borghese.

art.q: Which composer's 'L'Orfeo' (1607) is the earliest opera still regularly performed today?
art.fact: L'Orfeo was first performed at the court of the Gonzaga family in Mantua.

politics.q: How many consuls jointly led the Roman Republic each year?
politics.fact: Consuls served one-year terms, and Romans identified each year by naming the two consuls in office.

politics.q: What title did Benito Mussolini adopt as leader of Fascist Italy?
politics.fact: Mussolini was voted down by his own Fascist Grand Council in July 1943 and then arrested on the king's orders.

politics.q: The 1957 treaty that created the European Economic Community was signed in which city?
politics.fact: Six countries signed the Treaty of Rome on 25 March 1957, in a palace on the city's Capitoline Hill.

politics.q: Which Florentine diplomat wrote 'The Prince', a classic of political theory?
politics.fact: Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513 after being forced out of office in Florence; it was only published in 1532, after his death.

politics.q: In which year did Italians vote in a referendum to replace the monarchy with a republic?
politics.fact: King Umberto II reigned for only about a month, earning the nickname 'the May King', before leaving for exile in Portugal.

politics.q: What is the lower house of Italy's Parliament called?
politics.fact: The Chamber of Deputies meets in Palazzo Montecitorio, while the Senate sits in nearby Palazzo Madama.

politics.q: Which Roman palace is the official residence of the President of Italy?
politics.fact: The Quirinal was built as a summer residence for popes, then housed Italy's kings before becoming the presidents' home.

politics.q: Which 1929 agreement established Vatican City as an independent state?
politics.fact: Covering about 44 hectares, Vatican City is the smallest independent state in the world.

politics.q: On what date did the Constitution of the Italian Republic come into force?
politics.fact: One of the constitution's final provisions explicitly forbids re-forming the dissolved Fascist party in any form.

politics.q: Which former Prime Minister was kidnapped and killed by the Red Brigades in 1978?
politics.fact: Moro, five times Prime Minister, was seized in Rome in March 1978; his body was found in a car on Via Caetani that May.

politics.q: Which media tycoon served as Italy's Prime Minister four times between 1994 and 2011?
politics.fact: Berlusconi also owned AC Milan from 1986 to 2017, during which the club won five European Cup and Champions League titles.

politics.q: In the Roman Republic, what title was given to a magistrate granted supreme power for a short emergency?
politics.fact: According to tradition, Cincinnatus left his plough to serve as dictator in 458 BCE, then resigned after about two weeks.

politics.q: Italy was a founding member of which military alliance in 1949?
politics.fact: Italy hosts NATO's Allied Joint Force Command Naples, based near the city.

politics.q: What were the armed squads of Mussolini's Fascist movement commonly called?
politics.fact: Officially the Voluntary Militia for National Security, the Blackshirts copied the black uniform of the elite Arditi assault troops of the First World War.

politics.q: Which river did Julius Caesar cross with his army in 49 BCE, defying the Senate and starting a civil war?
politics.fact: Roman law forbade a general to lead his army into Italy proper; Caesar reportedly declared 'alea iacta est', 'the die is cast'.

politics.q: Which Roman statesman and orator exposed the Catiline conspiracy in 63 BCE?
politics.fact: Cicero's famous cry 'O tempora, o mores!' ('Oh the times, oh the customs!') comes from his first speech against Catiline.

politics.q: Which patriot founded the 'Young Italy' movement in 1831 to campaign for a united Italian republic?
politics.fact: Mazzini spent much of his life in exile, largely in London, and remained a committed republican even after Italy united as a monarchy.

politics.q: How long is the term of office of the President of the Italian Republic?
politics.fact: Presidents are elected by Parliament in joint session together with regional delegates, and must be at least 50 years old.

politics.q: Which Roman office was created to protect the plebeians and could veto the acts of magistrates?
politics.fact: Tribunes were sacrosanct, so harming one was a capital crime; the Gracchus brothers used the office to push land reform.

politics.q: Which party took part in every Italian government from 1946 until its dissolution in 1994?
politics.fact: The 'Tangentopoli' bribery scandal, uncovered by Milan's 'Clean Hands' investigation, helped bring about the party's collapse.

politics.q: Who became the first Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861?
politics.fact: Cavour died in June 1861, less than three months after the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed.

politics.q: Which liberal statesman served as Prime Minister five times between 1892 and 1921, giving his name to an era?
politics.fact: Giolitti's government introduced near-universal male suffrage in 1912.

politics.q: Which Italian Prime Minister was one of the 'Big Four' at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference?
politics.fact: Orlando walked out of the conference in protest when Italy's claim to the Adriatic port of Fiume was rejected.

politics.q: Which Communist leader proposed a 'historic compromise' with the Christian Democrats in the 1970s?
politics.fact: Under Berlinguer, the Italian Communist Party won about 34% of the vote in 1976, its best result ever.

politics.q: What was the name of Rome's first written law code, drawn up around 450 BCE?
politics.fact: Cicero recalled that as a boy he had to learn the Twelve Tables by heart, though the original tablets were later lost.

current-affairs.q: Who became Italy's first female Prime Minister in October 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Meloni leads Brothers of Italy, a party she co-founded in 2012 that topped the September 2022 general election.

current-affairs.q: Which team did Italy beat in the final of UEFA Euro 2020, played in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Italy won on penalties at Wembley; goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma was named player of the tournament.

current-affairs.q: Which former European Central Bank president became Italy's Prime Minister in February 2021?
current-affairs.fact: As ECB president in 2012, Draghi calmed markets by pledging to do 'whatever it takes' to preserve the euro.

current-affairs.q: Which Italian tennis player won the 2024 Australian Open men's singles title?
current-affairs.fact: Raised in German-speaking South Tyrol, Sinner was a champion junior skier; in June 2024 he became the first Italian to top the ATP singles rankings.

current-affairs.q: Which Italian rock band won the Eurovision Song Contest in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Måneskin, formed in Rome, won with 'Zitti e buoni'; the band's name means 'moonlight' in Danish.

current-affairs.q: Who was re-elected as President of Italy in January 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Mattarella became only the second Italian president to win a second term, after Giorgio Napolitano in 2013.

current-affairs.q: Which northern region was the epicentre of Italy's first COVID-19 wave in early 2020?
current-affairs.fact: The Lombard town of Codogno recorded Italy's first known locally transmitted COVID-19 case in February 2020.

current-affairs.q: Which architect designed Genoa's San Giorgio Bridge, opened in 2020 to replace the collapsed Morandi Bridge?
current-affairs.fact: Renzo Piano was born in Genoa and donated his design for the new bridge to his home city.

current-affairs.q: Italy hosted the June 2024 G7 leaders' summit in which southern region?
current-affairs.fact: The summit at Borgo Egnazia included Pope Francis, the first pope to take part in a G7 summit, who spoke about artificial intelligence.

current-affairs.q: In 2023, Italy won tennis's Davis Cup for the first time since which year?
current-affairs.fact: Italy beat Australia in the 2023 final in Málaga, with Jannik Sinner winning his key matches.

current-affairs.q: Which two Italian locations were chosen in June 2019 to host the 2026 Winter Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: The IOC picked Milan-Cortina over Sweden's Stockholm-Åre; Cortina had previously hosted the 1956 Winter Games.

current-affairs.q: In 2023, which club won Italy's Serie A title for the first time since 1990?
current-affairs.fact: Napoli's two earlier titles came in the Diego Maradona era; the club's stadium was renamed after him in 2020.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, Italy banned large cruise ships from sailing into the historic centre of which city?
current-affairs.fact: Approved in July 2021 to take effect that August, the ban came days before UNESCO was due to consider adding the city to its list of World Heritage in Danger.

current-affairs.q: Which Italian city hosted the Eurovision Song Contest in 2022?
current-affairs.fact: The contest was held in an arena built for the 2006 Winter Olympics, and was won by Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra.

current-affairs.q: Which Milan fashion designer, founder of his own world-famous label, died in September 2025 aged 91?
current-affairs.fact: He founded his company in 1975 with partner Sergio Galeotti, and dressed Richard Gere in the 1980 film 'American Gigolo'.

current-affairs.q: Which Italian sprinter won the men's 100 m at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, held in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Born in El Paso, Texas, to an American father and an Italian mother, Jacobs had been a long jumper before switching to sprinting.

current-affairs.q: Which country knocked Italy, the reigning European champions, out of World Cup qualifying in a March 2022 play-off?
current-affairs.fact: Having lost a play-off to Sweden for the 2018 tournament, Italy missed two World Cups in a row for the first time; a 2026 play-off loss to Bosnia and Herzegovina made it three.

current-affairs.q: Which country did Italy beat in the final to win the women's volleyball gold at the Paris 2024 Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: Coached by Julio Velasco, Italy won the final in straight sets, and Paola Egonu was named the tournament's most valuable player.

current-affairs.q: Which Italian astronaut commanded the International Space Station in 2019, the first Italian to do so?
current-affairs.fact: Samantha Cristoforetti followed him in 2022, becoming the first European woman to command the space station.

current-affairs.q: Which Italian city hosted the G20 leaders' summit in October 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Leaders at the summit endorsed a global minimum corporate tax rate of 15%.

current-affairs.q: In a September 2020 referendum, Italians approved cutting the number of elected members of Parliament from 945 to how many?
current-affairs.fact: From the 2022 election, the Chamber of Deputies shrank from 630 to 400 seats and the elected Senate from 315 to 200.

current-affairs.q: Which two Lombard cities shared the title of Italian Capital of Culture in 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Both cities were among the hardest hit by COVID-19 in 2020, and the shared title was awarded as a symbol of their recovery.

current-affairs.q: Which club beat Inter Milan 5-0 in the 2025 UEFA Champions League final?
current-affairs.fact: Played in Munich, it was the biggest winning margin ever recorded in a European Cup or Champions League final.

current-affairs.q: At the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, Italian Gianmarco Tamberi agreed to share the high jump gold with an athlete from which country?
current-affairs.fact: Offered a jump-off, Qatar's Mutaz Essa Barshim asked if they could both have gold, and the two friends embraced in celebration.

current-affairs.q: A strong earthquake swarm in May 2024 shook which volcanic caldera just west of Naples?
current-affairs.fact: Campi Flegrei is known for 'bradyseism', the slow rise and fall of the ground; parts of Pozzuoli have risen over a metre since 2005.

society.q: Which anti-poverty benefit, a flagship policy of the Five Star Movement, was introduced in Italy in 2019?
society.fact: The 'citizens' income' reached more than a million households at its peak; it was scrapped at the end of 2023 and replaced by a narrower scheme.

society.q: Italy's 'Superbonus', launched in 2020, offered homeowners a tax credit worth what percentage of the cost of energy-saving renovations?
society.fact: The scheme proved far more popular and costly than planned, with a bill to the state of well over €100 billion, and was wound down from 2023.

society.q: Italy is one of only a handful of EU countries that, as of 2025, has never had what?
society.fact: Most Italian pay is set by sector-wide collective agreements; a 2023 opposition proposal for a €9-an-hour minimum wage was rejected by parliament.

society.q: In April 2024 which Italian city became the first in the world to charge day-trippers an entry fee on busy days?
society.fact: The €5 charge applied on 29 peak days in 2024 and was extended to 54 days in 2025, with €10 for visitors who booked late.

society.q: What is the standard state retirement age in Italy, in force since 2019 and linked to life expectancy?
society.fact: Italy spends about 16% of GDP on pensions, one of the highest shares in the OECD, partly because of generous early-retirement schemes.

society.q: In October 2021 Italy became the first European country to require all workers to show what in order to enter their workplace?
society.fact: The pass showed vaccination, recovery or a recent negative test; workers without one faced suspension without pay.

society.q: In 2022 the number of births in Italy fell below what level for the first time since the country's unification?
society.fact: About 393,000 babies were born in 2022, against over a million a year in the 1960s; the total fertility rate stood at around 1.2 children per woman.

society.q: Italy was the largest single beneficiary of which EU programme, agreed in 2020 to help economies recover from the pandemic?
society.fact: Italy's national recovery plan (PNRR) was worth about €194 billion in grants and loans, to be spent on projects such as high-speed rail and digitalisation by 2026.

society.q: In autumn 2022 Italy's annual inflation rate peaked at roughly what level, the highest since the mid-1980s?
society.fact: ISTAT recorded 11.8% in October 2022, driven by energy bills; inflation then fell back below 1% by early 2024.

society.q: From January 2024 Italy's citizens' income was replaced by which benefit, limited mainly to households with children, over-60s or disabled members?
society.fact: People judged able to work were instead offered a smaller training allowance; the change cut the number of recipient households by hundreds of thousands.

society.q: Which country became Italy's largest supplier of natural gas in 2022, as Italy raced to replace Russian imports?
society.fact: Russia had supplied about 40% of Italy's gas before the invasion of Ukraine; Italy also signed deals with Qatar, Azerbaijan and Egypt and opened new floating LNG terminals.

society.q: In 2023 the unemployment rate among Italians aged 15 to 24 was roughly what?
society.fact: Youth unemployment had exceeded 40% in 2014; the 2023 figure of about 22% was the lowest in over a decade, though still well above the EU average.

society.q: Which world's-oldest bank, rescued by the Italian state in 2017, saw the Treasury begin selling down its stake in 2023?
society.fact: Founded in 1472, the bank cost taxpayers more than €5 billion to rescue; by 2024 the state's holding had fallen to around 12%.

society.q: According to the Interior Ministry, about how many migrants arrived in Italy by sea in 2023?
society.fact: The 2023 total of around 157,000 was the highest since 2016; arrivals fell by more than half in 2024.

society.q: In 2024 roughly what share of Italy's population was aged 65 or over, among the highest proportions in the world?
society.fact: Italy's median age was about 48, and ISTAT projected that over-65s would make up more than a third of the population by 2050.

society.q: In 2023 which EU country had the lowest employment rate for women?
society.fact: Only around 56% of Italian women aged 20 to 64 were in work, compared with an EU average of about 70%; in parts of the south the rate was below 40%.

society.q: In 2024 Italy's public debt stood at roughly what share of GDP?
society.fact: Only Greece had a higher ratio in the EU; the debt topped €3 trillion for the first time in 2024.

society.q: Which single monthly payment for families with children, replacing a patchwork of older bonuses and deductions, did Italy introduce in March 2022?
society.fact: The 'universal single allowance' is paid for each child up to the age of 21, with amounts varying by household income.

society.q: Italy's 'Quota 100' early-retirement scheme, in force from 2019 to 2021, allowed people to retire at 62 provided they had paid contributions for how many years?
society.fact: The name came from the two numbers adding up to 100; it was followed by 'Quota 102' in 2022 and 'Quota 103' (62 plus 41 years) in 2023.

society.q: In 2024 Italy doubled its annual flat tax on foreign income for wealthy new residents from €100,000 to what?
society.fact: The regime, introduced in 2017, had attracted several thousand wealthy foreigners, especially to Milan, prompting complaints about rising housing costs.

society.q: In 2023 Italy raised the turnover ceiling for its 15% flat-tax 'regime forfettario' for the self-employed from €65,000 to what?
society.fact: Around two million freelancers and small traders use the simplified regime, which charges 5% for the first five years of a new business.

society.q: In 2023 which major Italian bank became one of the first large employers in the country to offer staff a voluntary four-day working week?
society.fact: Staff could work four nine-hour days for the same pay, and the bank also expanded its remote-working arrangements.

society.q: ISTAT estimated that Italy's 'unobserved' or shadow economy was worth roughly what share of GDP in 2022?
society.fact: The estimate of around €200 billion covers undeclared work and tax evasion as well as illegal activities; undeclared workers numbered close to three million.

society.q: What name was given to the government-backed anti-inflation scheme of late 2023, in which Italian retailers agreed to discount a basket of everyday goods?
society.fact: The 'tricolour trolley' ran from October to December 2023; participating shops marked discounted goods with an Italian-flag sticker.

society.q: From January 2023 Italy raised its legal limit on cash payments to what amount, instead of letting it fall to €1,000 as previously planned?
society.fact: Italy has long tried to restrict cash to fight tax evasion; the limit had been cut to €2,000 in 2022 before the new government reversed course.

general.q: Which Italian city is built on more than 100 small islands in a lagoon?
general.fact: Venice spreads across 118 small islands linked by more than 400 bridges.

general.q: Which city is the traditional home of pizza?
general.fact: In 2017, UNESCO added the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

general.q: In which city does the famous Leaning Tower stand?
general.fact: The bell tower began leaning within a few years of building work starting in 1173, due to soft ground; it took about two centuries to finish.

general.q: Which active volcano towers over eastern Sicily?
general.fact: Etna is one of the world's most active volcanoes and was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013.

general.q: What is the longest river in Italy?
general.fact: The Po flows about 650 km from Monte Viso in the Alps to the Adriatic Sea, crossing Italy's most productive farmland.

general.q: Besides Vatican City, which independent country is completely surrounded by Italy?
general.fact: San Marino claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic, with a traditional founding date of 301 CE.

general.q: What is the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea?
general.fact: Sicily has been ruled by Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Normans and Spaniards, all of whom left traces in its food and architecture.

general.q: How many times has Italy's men's team won the FIFA World Cup?
general.fact: Italy won in 1934, 1938, 1982 and 2006; the 2006 final against France in Berlin was decided on penalties.

general.q: Which Italian region is home to Parmigiano Reggiano and traditional balsamic vinegar of Modena?
general.fact: Emilia-Romagna is also motor country: Ferrari, Lamborghini and Ducati are all based there.

general.q: The five Cinque Terre villages lie on the coast of which region?
general.fact: Of the five villages, only Corniglia does not sit directly on the sea; it perches on a clifftop instead.

general.q: Which ancient amphitheatre in Rome hosted gladiator fights?
general.fact: Officially the Flavian Amphitheatre, the Colosseum opened in 80 CE and could hold an estimated 50,000 spectators.

general.q: Into which Rome fountain do visitors traditionally toss a coin to ensure they will return?
general.fact: The coins, often worth more than a million euros a year, are collected and given to the Catholic charity Caritas.

general.q: Which mountain range runs along Italy's northern border?
general.fact: Mont Blanc, on the Italian-French border, is the highest peak in the Alps at about 4,800 metres.

general.q: Which two football clubs share Milan's San Siro stadium?
general.fact: San Siro is officially the Stadio Giuseppe Meazza, named after a 1930s star who played for both Milan clubs.

general.q: Italy's national sports teams are nicknamed 'Gli Azzurri' after the colour of their shirts. What colour is it?
general.fact: The blue comes from the royal House of Savoy, which ruled Italy from unification until 1946.

general.q: Which Tuscan city holds the Palio horse race around its Piazza del Campo?
general.fact: The Palio is run twice each summer, on 2 July and 16 August, and a horse can win even if it has lost its rider.

general.q: Chianti wine comes from which Italian region?
general.fact: Chianti Classico bottles carry a black rooster emblem, recalling a legend about settling a border dispute between Florence and Siena.

general.q: What is the second-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea?
general.fact: Sardinia is dotted with thousands of nuraghi, Bronze Age stone towers found nowhere else in the world.

general.q: What is the largest lake in Italy?
general.fact: Lake Garda's shores touch three regions, and its mild climate even lets lemons grow in terraced lemon houses.

general.q: Which Sicilian port gives its name to a famous fortified wine?
general.fact: English merchant John Woodhouse popularised Marsala in the 1770s, and Nelson's fleet later bought it in large quantities.

general.q: In which Italian region is French an official language alongside Italian?
general.fact: Italy has other protected languages too: German is co-official in South Tyrol, and Slovene is protected around Trieste.

general.q: Stromboli and Vulcano belong to which volcanic island group off Sicily?
general.fact: The island of Vulcano, which Romans believed was the forge of the god Vulcan, gave the world the word 'volcano'.

general.q: What is the name of the hot, often dusty wind that blows from North Africa across southern Italy?
general.fact: The scirocco can carry Saharan dust across the sea, which sometimes falls in Italy as reddish 'blood rain'.

general.q: Which ear-shaped pasta is the signature shape of Apulia (Puglia)?
general.fact: In Bari's old town, women still make orecchiette by hand at tables in the street, shaping each one with a thumb.

general.q: The Giro d'Italia leader's pink jersey matches the pink pages of which newspaper, which founded the race?
general.fact: The first Giro, in 1909, was won by Luigi Ganna; the leader's pink jersey, the maglia rosa, was introduced in 1931.
